title: Lamrim: karma
hookLine: actions have results; small actions can grow large

lines: DRIP: ONE DROP, TOO SMALL TO MATTER.
A WEEK LATER, A FULL BUCKET.
WHAT DOES TODAY ADD UP TO?
cards: Drip. A leaky tap over an empty bucket in the corner of a shed. Drip.
Nobody notices one drop; it's too small to matter. Drip. Come back in a week, and the bucket is full to the rim, maybe spilling onto the floor.
No single drop did it. All of them did. The Dhammapada uses almost exactly that picture, a water pot filled drop by drop, and the lamrim takes it up as its next stair.
If death is certain and its time unknown, what does what I do today actually add up to?

teach.b: You met karma as intention on day three hundred seventy-two; here it's the next stair. First, actions have results. Karma, in Buddhist teaching, means intentional action: what you do, say and think on purpose.
The lamrim teaches that such actions bring results in kind: kind actions tend toward happiness, harmful ones toward suffering.

teach.h: A POT FILLED DROP BY DROP.
teach.b: Not as a reward or a punishment handed down by anyone, but the way a seed becomes the plant it is. Second, small grows large.
The Dhammapada warns against thinking lightly of a harm, saying it won't come back to me, because a water pot fills from falling drops.

The next verse says the same of good: the wise fill up with good, gathered little by little. The lamrim adds a picture of its own: a tiny seed can become a huge tree. Third, two companions to that idea.
You don't meet the results of what you never did. And what you did do doesn't simply vanish because time passed.

Together they make the teaching practical: nothing small is wasted, in either direction. Fourth, why this follows death. If life is precious and its end unknown, a person might despair of ever doing anything big enough.
Karma answers: you don't have to. A held tongue, a shared lunch, a minute of patience in traffic, each one is a drop.
So are habits, and in this teaching, so are lives.

how: In lamrim practice, students reflect on how intentional actions bring results in kind and how small actions grow, then try to take care with small harms and small kindnesses in daily life.

o: the next stair: karma, where small actions grow large
the next stair: fate, a life written out in advance
the next stair: a reward or punishment from a judge

games.q: the karma stage: tap the pairs.

s: in this teaching, karma is a punishment handed down by someone
it works the way a seed becomes the plant it is, not as a sentence from a judge.
the Dhammapada warns against thinking lightly of small harms
it says a water pot fills from falling drops, and says the same of small goods.
only big actions count for karma
the lamrim teaches that small actions can grow large.

games.q: you're about to skip a small kindness because it seems too small to matter. what does today's stair say?
o: skip it: only big deeds count.
do it: small actions grow, and nothing small is wasted.
save it up for one big deed later.
games.why: the Dhammapada's water pot and the lamrim's seed say the same thing: small grows large, in both directions.

practice: Choose one small good deed, small enough that it will actually happen: a thank-you text, holding a door, putting away something someone else left out.
Picture yourself doing it, simply, then picture it as one drop going into a bucket, quiet, unremarkable, and real.

wordCard.voice: Lamrim, the next stair: karma. Intentional actions bring results in kind, and small actions can grow large. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: small grows large. No drop is too small to count. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 121 (small harms fill the pot drop by drop)
Dhammapada 122 (small goods fill it as well)
the stage on karma: results in kind, karma grows, unmet if not done, not lost
